title: Why are strings immutable in Java (security, string pool, thread safety, hashcode caching, safe sharing)?
shortTitle: Why are strings immutable in Java?

s1_definition.profdef: A `String` object in Java is immutable, meaning once it is created its character contents can never change; any method that appears to modify a string actually returns a new string. This design was chosen deliberately for several reasons: security, because strings carry sensitive parameters like file paths and connection URLs that must not change after validation; the string pool, which can safely share one instance of a literal across the whole program only because it cannot be mutated; thread safety, because an unchangeable object needs no synchronization; and hashcode caching, because an immutable string can compute its hash once and reuse it, which makes String an excellent HashMap key.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a string like an account number printed on a fixed metal plate at National Bank of India, rather than written in erasable pencil. Once Rajesh's account number SAV2001 is stamped, nobody can alter that plate; if you need a different number you make a new plate. Because the plate can never change, the bank can safely keep one master plate in a central drawer and let every department point at the same plate instead of making copies, no two clerks can secretly edit it behind each other's backs, and the filing index can memorize its location once and trust it forever.
s1_definition.oneliner: Strings are immutable so they can be safely pooled and shared, used as reliable map keys with a cached hash, trusted after security checks, and read by many threads without any locking.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `String` object in Java is immutable, meaning once it is created its character contents can never change; any method that appears to modify a string actually returns a new string. This design was chosen deliberately for several reasons: security, because strings carry sensitive parameters like file paths and connection URLs that must not change after validation; the string pool, which can safely share one instance of a literal across the whole program only because it cannot be mutated; thread safety, because an unchangeable object needs no synchronization; and hashcode caching, because an immutable string can compute its hash once and reuse it, which makes String an excellent HashMap key.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a string like an account number printed on a fixed metal plate at National Bank of India, rather than written in erasable pencil. Once Rajesh's account number SAV2001 is stamped, nobody can alter that plate; if you need a different number you make a new plate. Because the plate can never change, the bank can safely keep one master plate in a central drawer and let every department point at the same plate instead of making copies, no two clerks can secretly edit it behind each other's backs, and the filing index can memorize its location once and trust it forever.

**One line to remember:** Strings are immutable so they can be safely pooled and shared, used as reliable map keys with a cached hash, trusted after security checks, and read by many threads without any locking.

sections.s2_technical:
Immutability means the internal character data of a String never changes after construction. In modern Java the characters live in a private final byte array, and String exposes no method that mutates it. Methods like `substring`, `concat`, `replace`, and `toUpperCase` all return a brand new String and leave the original untouched. A classic trap is `s.concat(" World")` without reassigning the result; the original `s` is unchanged, which only makes sense once you internalize that strings cannot be modified in place.

The first reason is the string pool, also called the intern pool. String literals are interned, so every occurrence of the literal `"SAV2001"` in your code refers to the same single String object in the pool. This saves enormous memory in programs that use the same literals repeatedly. Sharing one instance is only safe because the instance cannot change; if one piece of code could mutate a pooled string, every other piece of code using that literal would be corrupted. A small example is `String a = "SAV2001"; String b = "SAV2001";` where `a == b` is true because both point to the same pooled object.

The second reason is security. Strings are used everywhere as parameters that get validated and then acted upon: file paths, class names loaded by a class loader, database connection URLs, and host names in network calls. If strings were mutable, an attacker could pass a validated-looking value and then mutate it after the security check but before the actual use, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use attack. Because the string cannot change, what you validated is exactly what you use. The third reason is thread safety: an immutable object has no writable state, so any number of threads can read the same String concurrently with no locks and no visibility problems, which matters in a high-throughput banking service where account identifiers fly between threads.

The fourth reason is hashcode caching and its consequence, safe use as a map key. Because the contents never change, String computes its hash code once on first request and caches it in a field, so repeated lookups in a HashMap are fast. More importantly, a key in a HashMap must not change its hash after insertion, or the map can never find it again; immutability guarantees a String key's hash is stable forever, which is why String is the most common and safest HashMap key. A senior nuance is that this is also why you should never store a password in a String: it lingers in the pool and in memory until garbage collected and cannot be wiped, so security-sensitive secrets use a char array that you can overwrite. Another nuance is that immutability enables safe sharing without defensive copying, so returning a String field from a getter needs no copy, unlike returning a mutable array or list.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India uses account numbers like SAV2001 as keys in an in-memory ledger map and as values repeated across thousands of records. If these account-number strings could change, the ledger lookups would break and memory would balloon. This is exactly what string immutability and the string pool solve, because the same literal is shared as one object and its hash stays stable as a map key.

Problem 2 — A transfer request carries a destination account number that the service validates for format and ownership, then uses to move money. If the string could be mutated between the validation and the transfer, an attacker could redirect funds. This is exactly what immutability prevents, because the validated string is guaranteed to be the same string that is used.

In the mini-project we build a `LedgerService` keyed by immutable account-number strings, demonstrate that interned literals are the same object, show that concat without reassignment leaves the original unchanged, and show a validate-then-use flow that is safe because the string cannot change. We also contrast a `char[]` for the PIN to show the security alternative.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two literal strings "SAV2001", an account-number key, a validated destination "CUR3001", and a four-character PIN.

Step 1: Two variables are assigned the literal "SAV2001". Because literals are interned, both point to the single pooled String object, so the identity comparison is true.

Step 2: `a.concat("-COPY")` runs. A new String "SAV2001-COPY" is created and returned, but it is not assigned back to `a`, so `a` still reads "SAV2001". The original is untouched because strings cannot change in place.

Step 3: The ledger registers accounts keyed by their immutable account-number strings. The HashMap computes each key's hash once and caches it, and because the key can never change, the hash stays valid, so later lookups find the right bucket.

Step 4: The destination "CUR3001" is validated by a map lookup and then used directly to credit 50,000. Because the string cannot change between the check and the use, the money goes exactly where it was validated to go.

Step 5: The PIN is stored in a char array and then overwritten with asterisks, something impossible with a String, demonstrating why secrets avoid String.

```text
[INFO] pool: a == b (same object)? true
[INFO] after concat, a is still: SAV2001 (new string was SAV2001-COPY)
[INFO] lookup SAV2001 balance = Rs.1000000
[INFO] validated CUR3001; using the SAME immutable string to transfer
[INFO] CUR3001 after credit = Rs.300000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text

                                        ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────┐
                         │ String Pool (interned)    │
                         │  "SAV2001"  (ONE object)  │  ← a and b both point here
                         └──────────────────────────┘
                                        │ immutable → safe to share
                                        ▼
  a.concat("-COPY") → NEW object "SAV2001-COPY"   (a unchanged)

  LedgerService map:  key "SAV2001" → hashCode cached once (stable)
    put → bucket by hash
    get("SAV2001") → same hash → found

  validate(dest="CUR3001") ─── same immutable string ──→ credit(dest, 50,000)
    (no mutation possible between check and use)
```

```text
  ═══ LLD — Why String is Immutable ═══

  ┌─ Reasons ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1 String pool: one shared instance per literal        │
  │ 2 Security: validated value can't change before use   │
  │ 3 Thread safety: no writable state → no locks         │

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ String (final class)                   │
  │  - value: byte[] (private FINAL)       │  never mutated
  │  - hash: int (cached)                  │  computed once
  │  + substring/concat/replace → NEW Str  │  non-mutating
  │  + hashCode(): reuse cached value      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Map key contract:
    key's hashCode MUST be stable after insertion
    String guarantees this (immutable) → ideal key

  Security note:
    password/PIN → use char[] (can be wiped),
    NOT String (lingers in pool/memory until GC)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A String in Java is immutable, which means once it is created its character contents can never change, and every method that looks like it modifies a string, such as substring, concat, or toUpperCase, actually returns a brand new string and leaves the original untouched. This was a deliberate design decision, and I can give five concrete reasons for it. The first is the string pool. String literals are interned, so every occurrence of a literal like the account number SAV2001 refers to the same single object in the pool, which saves a lot of memory. Sharing one instance across the whole program is only safe because that instance can never be mutated; if any code could change a pooled string, it would corrupt every other place that uses the same literal.

The second reason is security. Strings are used everywhere as parameters that get validated and then acted upon, like file paths, class names, and connection URLs. If strings were mutable, an attacker could pass a value that passes validation and then mutate it before it is actually used, which is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use attack. Because the string cannot change, what I validated is exactly what I use, and in my banking service that means a destination account number that passes the ownership check is guaranteed to be the same number the money is sent to.

The third reason is thread safety. An immutable object has no writable state, so any number of threads can read the same string concurrently with no locks and no visibility problems, which matters in a high-throughput banking system where account identifiers move constantly between threads. The fourth reason is hashcode caching and its consequence, safe use as a map key. Because the contents never change, String computes its hash code once and caches it, so repeated HashMap lookups are fast, and crucially the key's hash stays stable forever. A map key whose hash changed after insertion could never be found again, so immutability is exactly what makes String the safest and most common HashMap key. The fifth reason is safe sharing without defensive copying, so I can return a String field from a getter directly without worrying that the caller will mutate my internal state.

The senior nuance I always add is the flip side: because a String lingers in memory and the pool until garbage collected and cannot be wiped, you should never hold a password or a PIN in a String. For those secrets I use a character array, which I can overwrite with blanks the instant I am done, and that trade-off between convenient immutable identifiers and wipeable secret arrays is exactly the kind of detail that shows I understand why the design is the way it is.
